findings.title: Behavioral divergence: empty ts.skin_family_scope array now blocks instead of passes
findings.why_it_matters: The old guard (line 7006 of workbench.js pre-extraction) was `if (templateScope && templateScope.size && !templateScope.has(skinFamily)) return false` — an empty array produced a Set with size=0, templateScope.size was falsy, so the whole condition short-circuited to false and the action passed through. The new guard is `if (templateScope !== null && (!templateScope.size || !templateScope.has(skinFamily))) return false` — an empty array still produces size=0, but now `!templateScope.size` is true so the action is blocked. This is a behavior change on a previously-passing input, not just a refactor. The test suite exercises the empty-array case (line 203) and asserts `toBeFalse()`, meaning the tests are written to the new behavior, not the old one. If any real registry or template-set descriptor reaches `getEnabledActions` with `skin_family_scope: []`, actions that previously rendered will silently disappear.
findings.suggested_fix: Decide which behavior is correct for an empty skin_family_scope array (pass-through as before, or block as now), document the intent, and align test assertion and source code to that decision. If blocking is intended, note it as a deliberate breaking change in the commit message and add a fixture in the real registry to confirm no extant template-set uses [].
evidence: workbench.js pre-extraction line 7006: `if (templateScope && templateScope.size && !templateScope.has(skinFamily)) return false`
node -e confirms: old returns true for empty array + 'humanoid', new returns false
test line 203 asserts toBeFalse() for empty array, validating new behavior not old

findings.title: Behavioral divergence: non-empty template_actions + empty templateSetKey now blocks instead of passes
findings.why_it_matters: The old implementation entered the template_actions linking check only when `templateActions.length && templateSetKey` were both truthy. When templateSetKey was an empty string and template_actions had entries, the check was skipped and the function returned true. The new code splits the condition: if templateActions.length is truthy, it immediately checks `if (!tsk) return false`. Any action with a non-empty template_actions list and no active templateSetKey now returns false instead of true. The test at line 306 ('returns false when template_actions exist but templateSetKey is empty') asserts toBeFalse() — it documents the new behavior but provides no evidence that the old behavior was intentionally changed.
findings.suggested_fix: Audit whether any caller of the original `isTemplateActionAuthorable` relied on the pass-through when templateSetKey was empty but template_actions was populated. If the new stricter behavior is intentional, document it explicitly in a comment and in the commit. If not, restore the compound condition `if (templateActions.length && tsk)`.
evidence: workbench.js pre-extraction: `if (templateActions.length && templateSetKey) { ... if (!linked) return false; }`
node -e confirms: old returns true for tsk='' + non-empty templateActions, new returns false
test line 306 asserts toBeFalse() for this case, encoding new behavior

findings.title: toEqual, toStrictEqual, and toDeepEqual are identical implementations — type/prototype distinctions are untestable
findings.why_it_matters: All three assertion methods use `JSON.stringify` for comparison. This means they cannot distinguish `undefined` values (dropped by stringify), `NaN` (serialized to `null`), object prototype differences, or key order in nested structures. Any test that calls `toStrictEqual` signals intent to catch type or prototype mismatches, but will silently pass even when the actual value differs in those dimensions. For this module the risk is low because all returned values are plain objects and booleans, but the harness provides false confidence in tests that use `toStrictEqual` specifically. Future tests added to this file inherit the same silent gap.
findings.suggested_fix: Either rename all three to a single `toDeepEqual` (removing the semantic distinction), or implement `toStrictEqual` properly using recursive structural comparison that handles undefined, NaN, and prototype chain.
evidence: test lines 64-69: toStrictEqual body is identical to toEqual body (JSON.stringify comparison)
test lines 77-83: toDeepEqual body is identical to toEqual body
JSON.stringify({a: undefined}) === JSON.stringify({}) — key with undefined value is indistinguishable from missing key

findings.title: workbench.js wrapper functions are untested — window.__workbenchTemplateGating lookup failure has no test
findings.why_it_matters: The new workbench.js wrapper destructures `window.__workbenchTemplateGating` at IIFE load time. If the script tag order is wrong (workbench.js loaded before workbench-template-gating.js) or the browser export path fails for any reason, the destructuring will throw and the entire IIFE will fail silently. There is no test for this load-order contract, no test for the wrapper functions themselves, and no test that verifies the browser path sets `window.__workbenchTemplateGating` with the correct shape.
findings.suggested_fix: Add a test (or at minimum a load-guard assertion in workbench.js) that verifies `window.__workbenchTemplateGating` is populated with the expected keys before destructuring. Consider a defensive check: `if (!window.__workbenchTemplateGating) throw new Error('workbench-template-gating.js must be loaded before workbench.js')`.
evidence: workbench.js line 6995: `const { BUNDLE_ACTION_ORDER, isTemplateActionAuthorable: _isTemplateActionAuthorable, getEnabledActions: _getEnabledActions } = window.__workbenchTemplateGating;`
workbench-template-gating.js lines 93-99: browser export only sets window.__workbenchTemplateGating when typeof window !== 'undefined'

findings.title: No CI or npm test script wires the new test file — it is opt-in only
findings.why_it_matters: package.json scripts.test is still `echo 'Error: no test specified' && exit 1`. The new test file must be run manually via `node tests/web/workbench-template-gating.test.js`. It will not run on `npm test`, will not run in any CI pipeline using the standard Node test hook, and will not block merges. The 38 tests exist but provide no regression protection unless explicitly invoked.
findings.suggested_fix: Update package.json scripts.test to `node tests/web/workbench-template-gating.test.js` (or use a glob runner). Add CI step to invoke `npm test` so the gate fires on every push.

findings.title: getEnabledActions ordering test relies on JS object key insertion order — fragile across engines
findings.why_it_matters: The canonical ordering test (line 419) asserts `Object.keys(result)` equals `['idle','attack','death']` using `toDeepEqual` which uses `JSON.stringify`. Object.keys order is guaranteed to follow insertion order in V8 for string keys that are not array indices, but this is an implementation detail of V8, not a language guarantee for all JS environments. More critically, the assertion tests that `JSON.stringify(['idle','attack','death']) === JSON.stringify(Object.keys(result))`, which is key-order dependent. If getEnabledActions ever switches to a Map or a different accumulation strategy, the ordering test gives a false signal.
findings.suggested_fix: This is low risk in practice for Node.js, but note it explicitly. The real concern is that ordering tests coupled to JSON.stringify array comparison will silently pass out-of-order results if the expected array is also out of order. Consider asserting positional equality explicitly: `expect(keys[0]).toBe('idle')` etc., which the test already does for the non-canonical key case at lines 440-441.
evidence: test lines 419-421: `expect(Object.keys(result)).toDeepEqual(['idle','attack','death'])` uses JSON.stringify array comparison
getEnabledActions accumulates into plain object `out` using insertion order

residual_risks: The two behavioral changes (empty skin_family_scope array, empty templateSetKey with non-empty template_actions) are each tested — but the tests assert the NEW behavior. If the old behavior was correct for any real caller, those tests actively hide the regression by encoding the wrong expectation.

The test harness has no timeout or async guard. If any future test accidentally returns a Promise (e.g., an async function passed to `it`), the runner will mark it as passed immediately without awaiting resolution, providing false-positive coverage.

There is no integration test that verifies the full chain: workbench-template-gating.js loaded in browser context -> window.__workbenchTemplateGating populated -> workbench.js wrapper calls delegate correctly. The unit tests cover only the pure module.

JSON.stringify-based equality in the harness is order-sensitive for object keys. Tests asserting on result objects with multiple keys could produce false negatives if key order shifts, or false positives if both expected and actual have the same keys but wrong values that happen to stringify identically (e.g., undefined vs missing key).
testing_gaps: No test covers the load-order failure path: workbench.js destructures window.__workbenchTemplateGating at IIFE init; no test verifies the module throws or warns when this is undefined.
No test covers the browser export path: `window.__workbenchTemplateGating` assignment in workbench-template-gating.js line 98 is exercised by zero tests.

No test covers `isTemplateActionAuthorable` called with a non-string actionKey (e.g., number, object) — the function compares actionKey directly against `entry.action_key` string values without normalizing it.

No test covers `prefixSpec.authorable` being undefined (neither true nor false) — the check `prefixSpec.authorable === false` will pass through on `undefined`, which may be an unintended permissive default.
No test covers `familyScope.authorable` being undefined — same permissive default risk as above.

No test covers getEnabledActions with a registry that has no prefix_catalog key at all (only tested as null registry or null ts; the prefix_catalog-absent case is tested for isTemplateActionAuthorable but not directly for getEnabledActions as the entry point).
The test file is not wired into any CI or npm test invocation — all 38 tests are opt-in only.
